**Yes, such a function exists.**

## Construction

Let $\varphi:\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty)$ be a continuous bump function with $\varphi(0)=1$, $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]$, and $\varphi$ not identically zero (e.g. the triangular bump $\varphi(t)=\max(1-|2t|,0)$). For each $n\ge 1$ set
$$h_n=\frac1n,\qquad w_n=e^n,$$
and choose centers $x_n$ recursively so that the supports $I_n:=[x_n-\tfrac{w_n}{2},\,x_n+\tfrac{w_n}{2}]$ are pairwise disjoint and $x_n\to+\infty$; for instance
$$x_1=0,\qquad x_{n+1}=x_n+\frac{w_n+w_{n+1}}{2}+1.$$
Define
$$g(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}h_n\,\varphi\!\Big(\frac{x-x_n}{w_n}\Big),\qquad f(x)=g(x)+e^{-|x|}.$$

## Verification

**Positivity and continuity.** Since the $I_n$ are pairwise disjoint and $x_n\to\infty$, only finitely many terms of the series are nonzero on any bounded interval, so $g$ is continuous. Adding $e^{-|x|}>0$ gives $f>0$ everywhere, and $f$ is continuous.

**Vanishing at infinity.** If $x\to+\infty$ and $x\in I_n$, then $g(x)\le h_n=1/n\to 0$ (because $x\in I_n$ with $n\to\infty$ forces $n\to\infty$); if $x\notin\bigcup I_n$ then $g(x)=0$. Hence $g(x)\to 0$ as $x\to+\infty$, and $g\equiv 0$ on $(-\infty,x_1-\tfrac{w_1}{2}]$, so $g(x)\to 0$ as $x\to-\infty$. Since $e^{-|x|}\to 0$, we get $f(x)\to 0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$.

**Non-integrability of $f^p$ for every $p>0$.** Because $f\ge g\ge 0$,
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x)^p\,dx\;\ge\;\int_{\mathbb{R}} g(x)^p\,dx.$$
Using the disjointness of the $I_n$ and the substitution $u=(x-x_n)/w_n$,
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}} g(x)^p\,dx=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}h_n^{\,p}\,w_n\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}\varphi(u)^p\,du=C_p\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{e^n}{n^p},$$
where $C_p:=\int\varphi^p>0$ is a finite positive constant (since $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support). The series $\sum_{n\ge 1} e^n/n^p$ diverges for **every** $p>0$, because $e^n/n^p\to\infty$. Therefore
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x)^p\,dx=+\infty\qquad\text{for all }p>0.$$

## Conclusion

The function $f(x)=\sum_{n\ge 1}\frac1n\,\varphi\!\big(\frac{x-x_n}{e^n}\big)+e^{-|x|}$ is positive and continuous on $\mathbb{R}$, satisfies $f(x)\to 0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$, yet $f^p\notin L^1(\mathbb{R})$ for every $p>0$. The key mechanism is that the spike widths $w_n=e^n$ grow faster than any power of $n$, overwhelming the decay $h_n^p=n^{-p}$ of the heights for every fixed $p$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
